pr_title: drivers: rtc: Wrong alarm mask in rtc_alarm_get_time
pr_body:
Fixing the following issues:

1. The mask can be wrong if the alarm register is
set to a MAX value because the alarm bit is the
highest in the alarm register. The mask is now
generated by checking the AE_x bits in the time
registers.

2. Fixing possible NULL pointer exception in
alarm_set_time API. timeptr can be set to NULL
with mask 0 in the alarm_set_time function.
The regs variable for the I2C communication
is written with the correct value from timeptr
only when the right bit in the mask is set.

3. rv8263c8_alarm_set_time() now resets the
alarm status.

4. Interrupts are now enabled by using
rv8263c8_alarm_set_time() rather than when
setting an alarm callback.

Closes #76659
pr_comments: @fabiobaltieri I changed the logic for the `rv8263c8_alarm_get_time` functions because the logic was wrong.

I updated the drivers with the points from the discussion. I also found another possible bug. For `rtc_alarm_set_time()` the documentation says:

```
The timeptr param may be NULL if the mask param is 0
```

This can lead to a NULL pointer exception, because `regs` is filled with the values from `timeptr` which can be `NULL`. I moved the instructions to the conditional statements of each `mask` bit.
@bjarki-andreasen and @jakubtopic If I see it correctly the scenario with mask = 0 and timeptr = NULL isn't covered in the unit test. Otherwise this issue has been seen earlier.

Hm... The RTC test suite includes clearing the alarm time, so there is at least one call made with mask = 0 and timeptr = NULL. It likely wouldn't catch a potential null dereference, though.

In the `rtc_alarm_set_time()` in this driver, the null dereference issue wasn't originally present, until I suggested removing the condition checking if the mask is 0 :))

The other two mentioned issues could be covered by tests:
- Ensuring the interrupt output remains enabled after disabling and re-enabling the alarm using `rtc_alarm_set_time()`
- Verifying that `rtc_alarm_set_callback()` doesn’t disable the alarm unintentionally.

@bjarki-andreasen, could you please review the updated behaviour of `rv8263c8_alarm_set_time()`? Specifically how it controls the RTC's interrupt output. This version seems better to me, as it supports utilizing the interrupt output even if it isn't connected to the MCU's GPIO.

> @bjarki-andreasen, could you please review the updated behaviour of rv8263c8_alarm_set_time()? Specifically how it controls the RTC's interrupt output. This version seems better to me, as it supports utilizing the interrupt output even if it isn't connected to the MCU's GPIO.

I don't quite get how the interrupt output can be utilized if it is not connected :)

Since the alarm and update flags/events both use the same interrupt, the interrupt should always be enabled if either update or alarm callback is set. When either update or alarm trigger the interrupt, the driver should read the status (RV8263C8_REGISTER_CONTROL_2) register, check what actually triggered the interrupt (RV8263C8_BM_TF set and/or RV8263C8_BM_AF set), then call the update and/or alarm callbacks. If the alarm callback was not set, we don't need to clear RV8263C8_BM_AF since it can't trigger the interrupt, and we instead read/clear it when the `is_pending` API is called :)

Summarized, there should only be one work item for the one interrupt callback, which checks the status and handles both update and alarm events.

Sorry for changing the direction of this PR, no idea how we ended up here.

> I don't quite get how the interrupt output can be utilized if it is not connected :)

There is a use case, where the RTC's interrupt output is not connected to the MCU but to another component, like a power management IC. In this case interrupt gpios on the RTC node would not be present and if the `set_alarm_callback()` controls which events generate an interrupt signal, there would be no way to enable it.

There are already some drivers that always enable RTC's interrupt output when setting alarm:

- rtc_mc146818
- rtc_pcf8523 (when enabled using wakeup-source property)
- rtc_pcf8563

I think it should be unified, documented behaviour.

> If the alarm callback was not set, we don't need to clear RV8263C8_BM_AF since it can't trigger the interrupt, and we instead read/clear it when the is_pending API is called :)

I believe the correct behaviour is to (also) clear the alarm status when setting a new alarm time. Otherwise if an alarm is already pending, the newly set alarm may never trigger.

> Summarized, there should only be one work item for the one interrupt callback, which checks the status and handles both update and alarm events.

No changes there.

In this case interrupt gpios on the RTC node would not be present and if the `set_alarm_callback()` controls which events generate an interrupt signal, there would be no way to enable it.
> 
> > If the alarm callback was not set, we don't need to clear RV8263C8_BM_AF since it can't trigger the interrupt, and we instead read/clear it when the is_pending API is called :)

> I believe the correct behaviour is to (also) clear the alarm status when setting a new alarm time. Otherwise if an alarm is already pending, the newly set alarm may never trigger.
> 
> > Summarized, there should only be one work item for the one interrupt callback, which checks the status and handles both update and alarm events.
> 
> No changes there.

If I remember correctly @bjarki-andreasen and I have discussed this question in the initial PR for the RTC. Theoretically, you can handle the alarm and update stuff by using a thread or a worker to poll the status flags and call the callbacks from there. But IMO it´s not a good approach and we decided to discard this idea.

Let's move this question into a discussion. IMO It´s a valid use case and when working with a PMIC for low-power applications you don´t have a thread or worker to poll the status flags constantly. So there should be a more generic idea.

> Let's move this question into a discussion. IMO It´s a valid use case and when working with a PMIC for low-power applications you don´t have a thread or worker to poll the status flags constantly. So there should be a more generic idea.

I agree with moving the discussion. Conclusion for this PR is that it turns on interrupt output when setting an alarm, which supports the use case I mentioned and is also consistent with some existing drivers.

Now I'm catched up as well :) Regarding the interrupt, if it is not connected to the host, It makes sense to enable it (it has no negative impact) The reason for clearing the interrupt is to stop the IRQ from being called, which of course is only neccessary if the interrupt is connected :)

I'm okay with adding a note to the rtc_set_alarm_time API which states the interrupt always is enabled if it is not physically connected to the host :)
@bjarki-andreasen and @fabiobaltieri can you review it, please?

issue_context.title: Wrong mask generation in rtc_alarm_get_time in RV-8263 driver
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**

Two issues:

1. The `mask` can be wrong if the alarm register is set to a `MAX` value because the alarm bit is the highest in the alarm register.

2. Disabling the alarm callback must also disable the alarm flags in the alarm time registers because otherwise `rtc_alarm_get_time` will return a wrong mask.

review_comments: Please also remove the `MAX_x` and `MIN_x` defines. They are no longer used and could misleading.
